newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.S. "unilateralism" under fire at United Nations.
newsitem.headline: U.S. "unilateralism" under fire at United Nations.

text.p: From Canada to Malaysia, Norway to Gambia, the United States came under fire at the U.N. General Assembly this year for trying to dominate the United Nations while refusing to pay for it.

Speakers at the annual three-week debate that ended last week turned up the anti-American rhetoric with criticism ranging from missile attacks against Iraq to U.S. laws to punish foreigners doing business in Cuba or Iran and Libya.
While the United States was not the major theme in more than 181 scripted speeches, charges of so-called American unilateralism by the Clinton administration turned into a steady drumbeat.

The tone was set as soon as the debate opened on September 23 when Brazil's Foreign Minister Luiz Felipe Lampreia, the first speaker, said that "to stifle the U.N. little by little by depriving it of the means to perform its functions is no way to secure greater administrative efficiency."
Despite a recent infusion of cash, the United States will still owe about $1.3 billion by the end of the year.

Canada's Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy was even more blunt. He said withholding dues was a "form of blackmail." And Norwegian Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland said members could not "accept intimidation," adding that "withholding legally assessed contributions amounts to just that."

Gambia's Minister of Public Works, Communications and Information, Ebrihima Ceesay, said that "member countries should desist from withholding their contributions for purely political considerations."

Referring to Washington's successful efforts to get a zero-growth U.N. budget, Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas said that "no organisation can be reformed by starving it. Ironically, the countries that are pressing the hardest for cutbacks and reforms have themselves refused to finance the new austerity budget."

Among U.S. allies in Europe, France was most outspoken about U.S. "unilateralism" in trade. Said Foreign Minister Herve de Charette: "France and Europe do not accept that one country, even if it is the most powerful, is trying to regulate world trade by itself.

"The World Trade Organisation does not allow it and no one should doubt the firmness of French and European reactions," he said, referring to legislation that would allow naturalised Americans to sue, in U.S. courts, foreign companies deemed to have profited from property confiscated by Havana since the Cuban revolution of 1959.

Several Islamic countries, including Middle Eastern nations, said the firing of U.S. missiles at Iraq was neither authorised by the United Nations nor warranted after Baghdad's troops went into Iraq's Kurdish provinces.
"The undue and unwarranted use of force cannot restore rights or rectify wrong-doings," said Egypt's Foreign Minister Amr Moussa.

In a stinging attack on both the United States and Russia, Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said: "One great power continues its vendetta against Iraq, firing missiles at distant targets ... oblivious to the suffering of the besieged Iraqi people. Another power has shut the gates of mercy on the Chechnyans and with rockets and bombs have killed indiscriminately."

Added to the list of grievances is smouldering anger from many developing countries about the unceremonious way the United States has gone about opposing a second five-year term for Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali during a U.S. presidential election year.

About 30 states, mainly from Africa and the Middle East, openly endorsed Boutros-Ghali for a second term while another 71 praised him. The others were silent in the debate that included 12 heads of state, 17 prime ministers, 17 deputy prime ministers and 106 foreign ministers.
U.S. officials have made clear they will use their veto power in the Security Council to prevent his re-election and are tryng to persuade delegates to choose an alternative.

But judging from discussions so far, diplomats say that those supporting Boutros-Ghali, including France, are not expected to make the U.S. task an easy one. This includes turning down any candidate favoured by the United States.
